definition: Arabic is one of the major languages that have been given attention by machine translation (MT) researchers since the very early days of MT and specifically in the U.S.
details: The language has been considered "due to its morphological, syntactic, phonetic and phonological properties [to be] one of the most difficult languages for written and spoken language processing."

explainer.lead: Arabic machine translation is the automatic translation of text or speech between Arabic and other languages. It is a long-running research challenge because Arabic word forms, sentence structure, sounds, and sound patterns can all be difficult for computers to process.

tiers.eli5: Imagine turning a message written in Arabic into the same message in English without asking a person to translate it. A computer must work out what the Arabic words mean and how they fit together, then build a sensible sentence in the other language. Arabic makes this especially tricky because its words and sentences can have complicated structures.
tiers.practitioner: Arabic machine translation is applied to written or spoken language, with systems expected to handle Arabic morphology and syntax as well as phonetic and phonological properties where speech is involved. Evaluation should include difficult Arabic word forms and sentence structures rather than relying only on simple examples. Fluency alone is not enough: a plausible output can still fail to represent the Arabic input correctly.
tiers.paperLevel: Arabic machine translation concerns computational translation involving Arabic, a language studied since the early days of machine translation research, particularly in the United States. Its central difficulty lies in processing Arabic morphological, syntactic, phonetic, and phonological properties. These challenges affect both written and spoken language processing.

explainer.example: Given an Arabic sentence to translate into English, the system first analyzes its word forms and grammatical relationships rather than translating word by word. It then produces an English sentence intended to carry the same meaning.

usedIn.name: Machine translation research
usedIn.detail: Arabic has received attention from MT researchers since the field's early days, particularly in the United States.

usedIn.name: Written language processing
usedIn.detail: Arabic morphology and syntax present difficulties when automatically processing and translating text.

usedIn.name: Spoken language processing
usedIn.detail: Phonetic and phonological properties add challenges when translation involves speech.

explainer.intuition: Translation requires more than replacing each Arabic word with a word from another language: the system must interpret complex word forms and grammatical relationships, then express the same meaning naturally.
howItWorks: Receive Arabic input as written text or spoken language.
Analyze the input's word structure and sentence structure; speech also requires handling sound-related properties.
Work out how the interpreted content can be expressed in the target language.
Generate the translation while preserving the input's meaning.
explainer.whyItMatters: Better Arabic machine translation would improve automatic communication involving a major language. Its difficulty also makes it an important test of whether language-processing systems can handle complex word forms, grammar, and sounds.
misconceptions: It is not simply a matter of looking up each Arabic word in a bilingual dictionary.
The challenges are not limited to written text; spoken Arabic processing also involves phonetic and phonological difficulties.
A fluent-sounding translation is not necessarily a faithful one.
